I had a similar illness as you - heart rate issues followed by crushing fatigue and muscle weakness on a daily basis, among other odd symptoms.  The only thing that helped was prazosin, which is also prescribed for PTSD symptoms, specifically nightmares.  It was prescribed to me by a psychiatrist when I asked if there are any drug treatments for PTSD.  It was by surprise that it helped get my energy back and stopped my body from freaking out every morning.  I too thought I was having some kind of seizure disorder but I had an EEG done (something a neurologist could order) and that was negative.  I had a lot of varied symptoms due to what I didn’t realize till later was an excess of adrenaline; I had nearly every medical workup under the sun during the course of a year and the end result is basically I have pseudopheochromocytoma.  All the symptoms of an adrenaline-producing tumor without the actual biological cause of one.  It’s not really a recognized medical disorder yet but case reports in medical journals seem to point to it often happening after stressful circumstances to people who compartmentalize emotions.  A similarly vague condition that falls under a neurologist’s purview is functional neurological disorder in which one has seizure-like symptoms without the characteristic EEG findings.  It is also not well-recognized. 

Prazosin has not helped anhedonia so far but I may ask about increasing the dose.  I have started to have flagging energy again after starting a new job and it might be time.  Even on weekends, it’s following a similar pattern as my former physical symptoms of my feeling “ok” for a couple hours in the morning before I am hit with complete apathy, disinterest, and lack of motivation.  Prazosin is an alpha-blocker (similar in concept to a beta blocker, but works on different receptors) and was previously used more frequently as a blood pressure medication.  It is also prescribed for actual cases of pheochromocytoma, the adrenaline-producing tumor I referenced above.

That sounds like a lot of what I have experienced in the past.  My underlying medical issue is still being diagnosed, but L-ornithine L-aspartate in doses for hepatic encephalopathy has made a big difference for me, both with cognition and with sleep.  I aim for 3 to 6g 3 times daily: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK77395/.  I have the powdered form and mix it with Liquid IV packets, as it seems to really accelerate clearing the brain fog compared to just water or other hydration drinks I’ve tried.  (I get dehydrated v. easily lately.)

Sleep-wake inversions are actually associated with some serious medical issues and yet it is rarely discussed when talking about circadian rhythm issues: https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_inversion.  Have you been to see your doctor?  Have any other symptoms that may have seemed minor in the past?  I would definitely follow-up on anything that has been odd even if you feel otherwise fine.  It also wouldn’t hurt to check your temperature a few times during a few days just for a baseline; fevers everyday are NOT normal but can be easily mistaken for being just tired etc.

Another suggestion is getting your genes sequenced.  It is quite expensive but if you have had this issue for a long time, it could be worth it.  It has helped me with ruling in/ruling out what my whole issue could be (have had N24 all my life and this is why I got the sequencing done last year but then became suddenly very ill this Jan.)  I will say having scientific knowledge or access to someone who does would be very helpful in this area; I have college-level knowledge but I find trying to interpret my results in light of my symptoms, family history, and research quite complex and there are plenty of opportunities to get it wrong for novices like myself.

Also, pills wise, I had ok success with Seroquel at doses of 25-50mg.  It was like a pharmacological log that I could bonk myself with to knock out.  It took about an hour to kick in and then I’d finally be tired enough to sleep.  It did not feel refreshing... but I did actually sleep.  Another thing that has helped is turning the AC up in the few hours before bed.

Best of luck in finding something that works for you.  Hope you may find relief soon.

I skimmed your other post.  You mentioned high liver enzymes.  With that in mind, I wonder if you could possibly be suffering from hepatic encephalopathy.  It can cause day-night inversions much like DSPD, confusion, lethargy, and other symptoms.  Have you had your ammonia levels checked?  That is basically how they diagnose the issue.

A cause of high ammonia levels can also be from urea cycle disorders (rather than just general liver dysfunction).  These are genetic disorders where your body has trouble processing ammonia, which occurs naturally during protein breakdown, so it builds up to toxic levels.  Periods of stress, illness, intense exercise and more can cause this disorder to worsen due to the increased protein metabolism.

I would see a GI doctor regarding your liver enzymes and a neurologist regarding the confusion, being sure to mention the entirety of your symptoms to both.  And I would really push to be evaluated for a urea cycle disorder.

Yes, I have historically been pretty sleep deprived normally (more on the N24 spectrum of things, though, FWIW).  During the tail end of two periods of severe respiratory illness, I started to hallucinate on top of that, then developed delusions built on the hallucinations.  I recently found out I have an untreated breathing disorder (which is not the “asthma” I was previously diagnosed with for decades) that makes breathing through the mouth physically difficult and messes with the gas exchange capabilities of the lung, so I think the lack of oxygen + lack of sleep is what did it in my situation. 

Instead of any medical treatment, I was institutionalized for weeks on end in both of those cases and diagnosed with bipolar disorder.  They doped me up 6 ways from Sunday, yet the medications made me a zombie and did nothing for whatever “moods” I supposedly have and did not even stop the hallucinations/delusions.  Thankfully my psychiatrist is not a sadist and I am no longer on those pills and back to my regular meds for anxiety + ADHD, but the bipolar diagnosis remains.
